rubrics.criterion: In every TLS-bearing KV generation, the server-side session material (certificate, private key, optional client-CA) is owned by a named session value or type that loads and validates it in one place, and no stage of that generation's server connection path receives the three pieces as separately enumerated adjacent parameters.
rubrics.rationale: The server identity bundle is one half of this case's recurring group; it currently travels parameter by parameter through the configure/accept/stream-conversion stages of each generation, so resolving the case means giving that bundle one owner on this side of each generation, not in just one.

rubrics.criterion: In every TLS-bearing KV generation, the client-side session material (optional identity pair, optional server CA) is owned by a named session value or type, and no client-side stage (session configuration build, connector construction, connect step) enumerates the pieces as separate adjacent parameters.
rubrics.rationale: The client identity bundle is the other half of the recurring group and recurs in the same multi-stage pattern; a repair that folds only the server side leaves the documented client-path symptom untouched.

rubrics.criterion: In the configuration-driven generation, the session values are built once at startup from the TLS section of the configuration, and a single owner value (with whatever shared ownership the async hand-off needs) is handed into the server startup path and onward into the per-connection handler, replacing the per-item parameter chain that copied the material for every accepted connection.
rubrics.rationale: That generation was the widest traversal in the case: the material crossed config deconstruction, listener bootstrap, and the spawned per-connection task with widened shared-string types; an owner that stops at the bootstrap but still splays the group at the connection hand-off has not resolved the instance.

rubrics.criterion: No generation ends up with three or more sibling free functions that still enumerate the same identity/trust material as adjacent parameters under new or reordered names.
rubrics.rationale: A cosmetic pass (renaming the group members, shuffling their order, or re-splitting them into a differently named tuple) keeps the recurrence that makes this case a problem, so it must be detected as an unresolved repair rather than credited.

rubrics.criterion: The request-driven generations' server and client binaries build their session value once per process - outside the accept loop and outside the connect attempt - and reuse it for each connection, keeping each binary's existing connection structure and CLI surface intact.
rubrics.rationale: The binaries are the call sites where the group was re-listed at every connection; adapting them to construct once and reuse is the caller-side half of the re-homing, and their flags and connection behavior are the user-visible shape that must not be redesigned away.

rubrics.criterion: Each generation's network module surface is coherent after the change: it advertises the new session owner (or its constructors) it actually means to expose, and no re-export line still names removed helpers or stale symbols.
rubrics.rationale: The module re-exports are each generation's advertised helper surface; leaving a mix of removed free functions and new types makes the generations' public contracts incoherent, which downstream course code relies on.

rubrics.criterion: The multiplexing generations' local server fixtures construct or receive the folded session owner instead of accepting and forwarding the certificate/key/CA pieces as separate string parameters.
rubrics.rationale: Those fixture helpers set up real TLS listeners for the contribution tests and mirror the same bundle; a repair that leaves them splashing parameters keeps the pattern alive in a second consumer inside the same crates.

rubrics.criterion: Free helper functions made obsolete by the session owner - the per-layer configuration re-builders and the stream-conversion helpers that existed only to thread the loose pieces - are removed from each generation rather than left sitting unused beside the new types.
rubrics.rationale: Leaving the old free-parameter helper families in place next to a new owner keeps two competing ways to do the same handshake step and preserves the very plumbing this task retires; deletion, not coexistence, is the complete cleanup.

rubrics.criterion: No leftover debris from the re-homing remains in the affected crates: unused imports, unused fixture constants, or forwarding shims that merely keep old parameter-list call signatures alive alongside the new design.
rubrics.rationale: The case deliberately touched re-export lines, fixture constants, and helper signatures; an incomplete repair tends to leave exactly these small corpses behind, and their presence is a concrete marker of an unfinished pass.

rubrics.criterion: Per-generation trust policies are not swapped or unified: the newest generation still uses a configured CA in place of the system root store on its client side, while the earlier generations still add the CA on top of the system roots, and no generation's policy silently flipped to the other behavior.
rubrics.rationale: The generations intentionally differ in this exact semantic, and the difference is easy to destroy while folding owners (a shared helper that always does one of the two); flipping it changes which servers a given config trusts and is a case-specific functional regression the mainstream suite does not assert.

rubrics.criterion: Mutual-TLS gates keep their current direction: a server requires a verified client certificate only when a client-CA is configured, and a client installs its identity only when the pair is present - no repair forces client auth on everywhere or drops it where it was active.
rubrics.rationale: The optional-identity/optional-CA branches are central to how these generations differ; collapsing the gating either way changes who can talk to whom and breaks behaviors the case declares stable.

rubrics.criterion: Handshake outcomes are preserved exactly: connecting with an unfitting server name still fails the handshake, plain TLS sessions that work today still work, and multiplex sessions still come up over TLS in all four generations.
rubrics.rationale: These are the observable TLS behaviors the shipped tests actually assert for this stack; any drift here is a direct user-visible regression of the secure transport the task is supposed to keep intact.

rubrics.criterion: The fix does not reintroduce per-connection parsing: certificate/key material is not re-read and re-parsed inside the accept path for every individual connection, and malformed material surfaces at startup construction rather than mid-accept.
rubrics.rationale: One documented motivation for the case was parse-once reuse; a repair that quietly restores per-connection parsing trades a structural fix for a performance and error-handling regression the current design explicitly avoids.
